title: awk and sed: columns and edits
summary: awk reads a file as columns and can add them up; sed prints or changes lines. The two classics of text work.

text: awk cuts every line into fields, at the spaces, and runs your little program on each line.
- $1 is the first field, $2 the second, $0 the whole line.
- Unlike cut, several spaces in a row count as one separator.
- Put the program in single quotes, so the shell leaves $2 alone.

scheme: $2 == "pear"  only lines where this is true
END { … }     once, after the last line
text: An awk program is pattern { action }: the action runs only on the lines where the pattern is true.
- Variables start at 0: no need to set s first.
- END runs after the last line: the place to print a total.
sed reads a file line by line. Normally it prints every line; -n makes it quiet, and p prints the lines you pick.
- sed -n '/error/p' prints the lines that match, like grep.

scheme: │ │   │   └─ g: every match on a line
text: s/old/new/ replaces text. Without g, only the first match of each line changes.
- sed prints the result and leaves the file alone. -i edits the file in place.
- Try it without -i first: you see the result, and nothing is changed yet.
